title: Domains and Ranges of Radical Quotients
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Let f(x) = 1 and g(x) = 1 + sqrt(x). Determine the natural domains and ranges of f, g, the quotient f / g, and the quotient g / f.
finalAnswer: D_f = (-\infty, \infty),\ R_f = \{1\};\quad D_g = [0, \infty),\ R_g = [1, \infty);\quad D_{f/g} = [0, \infty),\ R_{f/g} = (0, 1];\quad D_{g/f} = [0, \infty),\ R_{g/f} = [1, \infty)

steps.title: Find the Domains and Ranges of f and g
steps.explanation: The constant function f(x) = 1 has domain (-infinity, infinity) and range {1}. For g(x) = 1 + sqrt(x), the square root requires x >= 0, and since sqrt(x) >= 0 takes all values in [0, infinity), adding 1 shifts the range to [1, infinity).
steps.why: The principal square root has domain [0, infinity) and range [0, infinity), so 1 + sqrt(x) has range [1, infinity).

steps.title: Determine the Domain and Range of f / g
steps.explanation: The intersection D_f cap D_g is [0, infinity), and on this interval g(x) = 1 + sqrt(x) >= 1 != 0, so D_{f/g} = [0, infinity). As 1 + sqrt(x) increases continuously from 1 (at x = 0) to infinity, its reciprocal 1/(1 + sqrt(x)) decreases continuously from 1 toward 0 (without reaching 0), giving range (0, 1].
steps.why: The reciprocal map u -> 1/u maps [1, infinity) bijectively onto (0, 1].

steps.title: Determine the Domain and Range of g / f
steps.explanation: Since f(x) = 1 is never zero, dividing g(x) by f(x) leaves 1 + sqrt(x) unchanged on D_f cap D_g = [0, infinity). Consequently, D_{g/f} = [0, infinity) and R_{g/f} = [1, infinity).
steps.why: Dividing by the constant 1 preserves both the domain intersection and the output values of g.
